title: Chapter 18: The binomial theorem and Pascal’s triangle

questions.stem:
By using the fact that \((1+x)^{11}=(1+x)^3(1+x)^8\). Show that

\(\binom{11}{5}=\binom85+\binom31\binom84+\binom32\binom83+\binom82\)
questions.hint: Equate the coefficient of x⁵ on both sides.

steps.explain: Compare the coefficient of \(x^5\) on both sides. On the left, by the binomial theorem:
On the right, write both expansions.
An \(x^5\) term comes from \(x^j\) in the first times \(x^{5-j}\) in the second, for \(j=0,1,2,3\).

questions.answer: Coefficient of x⁵ on the left: \(\binom{11}{5}\). On the right, x⁵ arises from x^j (from (1+x)³) times x^{5−j} (from (1+x)⁸), j = 0…3: \(\binom30\binom85+\binom31\binom84+\binom32\binom83+\binom33\binom82\). Since \(\binom30=\binom33=1\), equating gives the result.

keyPoints.note: Find the x⁵ coefficient on each side of (1 + x)¹¹ = (1 + x)³(1 + x)⁸.

questions.hint: Expand each combination using \({}^{n}C_2=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\) then subtract.

meta.source: Barker College 2023 Year 11 Preliminary Mathematics Extension 1

questions.stem: Consider the expression \((1+x)^n=\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{1}x+\binom{n}{2}x^2+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}x^n\). Multiplying by \(x\), another identity is obtained: \(x(1+x)^n=\binom{n}{0}x+\binom{n}{1}x^2+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}x^{n+1}\). Find the function \(F(n)\) such that \(2\binom{n}{1}+3\binom{n}{2}+4\binom{n}{3}+\cdots+n\binom{n}{n-1}=(n+2)F(n)\).
questions.answer: Differentiate both sides of the second identity: LHS = (1+x)^n + nx(1+x)^(n−1); RHS = 1 + 2C(n,1)x + 3C(n,2)x² + … + (n+1)C(n,n)xⁿ. Put x = 1: 2ⁿ + n2^(n−1) = 1 + 2C(n,1) + 3C(n,2) + … + n·C(n,n−1) + (n+1). So the required sum = 2^(n−1)(n+2) − (n+2) = (n+2)(2^(n−1) − 1), giving F(n) = 2^(n−1) − 1.
questions.hint: Differentiate the identity \(x(1+x)^n=\ldots\) with respect to \(x\) (product rule), then substitute \(x=1\).

steps.explain: Differentiate the right side term by term (each \(x^{k+1}\) gives \((k+1)x^k\)).

keyPoints.note: Differentiate the second identity and substitute \(x=1\).

meta.source: Baulkham Hills High School 2020 Year 11 Yearly Examination Mathematics Extension 1

questions.stem: Use the identity \((1+x)^{m}(1+x)^{n}=(1+x)^{m+n}\) to show that \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}=\dbinom{n}{4}+\dbinom{n}{3}\dbinom{m}{1}+\dbinom{n}{2}\dbinom{m}{2}+\dbinom{n}{1}\dbinom{m}{3}+\dbinom{m}{4}\). Which working is correct?
options: Coefficient of \(x^{4}\) on the left: \(\dbinom{m}{0}\dbinom{n}{4}+\dbinom{m}{1}\dbinom{n}{3}+\dbinom{m}{2}\dbinom{n}{2}+\dbinom{m}{3}\dbinom{n}{1}+\dbinom{m}{4}\dbinom{n}{0}\) (pairs of terms whose powers add to 4). On the right: \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}\). Equate and use \(\dbinom{m}{0}=\dbinom{n}{0}=1\).
Coefficient of \(x^{4}\) on the left: \(\dbinom{m}{4}+\dbinom{n}{4}\) (the \(x^{4}\) terms of each bracket). On the right: \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}\). So \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}=\dbinom{m}{4}+\dbinom{n}{4}\).
Coefficient of \(x^{4}\) on the left: \(\dbinom{m}{4}\dbinom{n}{4}\) (multiply the two \(x^{4}\) terms). On the right: \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}\). So they are equal.
Coefficient of \(x^{4}\) on the left: \(\dbinom{m}{1}\dbinom{n}{3}+\dbinom{m}{3}\dbinom{n}{1}\) only (the odd-power pairs). On the right: \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}\).
questions.hint: Find the coefficient of \(x^{4}\) on BOTH sides of the identity. In \((1+x)^{m}(1+x)^{n}\), each \(x^{4}\) arises from \(x^{r}\) in the first bracket and \(x^{4-r}\) in the second, for \(r=0,1,2,3,4\).

steps.explain: Binomial expansions: the general terms are \(\dbinom{m}{r}x^{r}\) in \((1+x)^{m}\) and \(\dbinom{n}{s}x^{s}\) in \((1+x)^{n}\).
On the right-hand side \((1+x)^{m+n}\) the coefficient of \(x^{4}\) is \(\dbinom{m+n}{4}\).
The two sides of an identity are equal for all \(x\), so their coefficients of \(x^{4}\) are equal. Use \(\dbinom{m}{0}=1\) and \(\dbinom{n}{0}=1\).

Rearrange the products to the order in the question (multiplication is commutative). Why not the others: B adds instead of combining the products; C multiplies the \(x^{4}\) terms (which gives \(x^{8}\)); D leaves out terms.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Equate the coefficient of x to the 4 on both sides; pairs of powers adding to 4.

meta.source: Frensham School 2021 Year 12 Trial HSC Examination Mathematics Extension 1
